_comment: English profile, for learners practising English. Voices: en-US tiffany/matthew, en-GB amy, en-AU olivia, en-IN kiara/arjun. tiffany and matthew are the polyglot voices and can speak every language Nova 2 Sonic supports.
_nativeLanguageNote: Target and native language are both English here, which makes the 'switched to their own language' part of the conversation prompt a no-op — harmless, but if you know your learners' first language, set nativeLanguage to it so coach notes are written in a language they read comfortably.
_localeComment: BCP-47 codes for Amazon Transcribe, which gives the coaching lane an independent transcript and identifies which language was actually spoken. Streaming identification needs at least two options, one dialect each.
_espeakComment: espeak-ng voice used to phonemise the transcript into EXPECTED phonemes. It must match the language being taught: phonemising English text with the Spanish voice turns "Hello" into "e ʎ o", which makes the comparison against what Wav2Vec2 actually heard meaningless.
_genderComment: Must match the voice: gendered languages conjugate self-reference. Feminine voices: tiffany, amy, olivia, kiara, ambre, beatrice, tina, lupe, carolina. Masculine: matthew, arjun, florian, lorenzo, lennart, carlos, leo.
regionalVariation: rhotic and non-rhotic "r" (American and Irish versus most British, Australian and New Zealand speech)
"t" as a glottal stop or as a tap between vowels ("butter" toward "budder")
the trap/bath and cot/caught vowel splits, which differ by region
"th" as f, v or d in some varieties
dropped "h" at the start of words
regional vocabulary and spelling conventions across all varieties
_learnerErrorsComment: The other side of the coin from regionalVariation: mistakes learners genuinely make that must NOT be excused as accent. Without these the reviewer treats almost everything as dialect and stays silent.
learnerErrors: replacing "th" with f, d, s or t so words merge (three / free, this / dis)
dropping or adding syllables in consonant clusters (strength, sixths)
confusing short and long vowel pairs that change the word (ship / sheep, full / fool)
stressing the wrong syllable so the word becomes hard to place
pronunciationExample: your "th" in "three" came out as "f", so it sounded like "free"
grammarExample: "I have lived here for two years" — the present perfect covers a stretch of time running up to now
